title: If You Must Punish, Design Punishments That Make People Better
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Following on from the penalty-versus-punishment distinction, this piece addresses the rarer cases where punishment — rather than a pre-set penalty — is genuinely warranted, typically for one-off or unusual infractions. The author's central design principle is that an effective punishment should build a skill or add value to the person, not merely inflict an unpleasant consequence, contrasting an essay assignment (which builds writing skill) against generic penalties like running laps. This reframes punishment design as a creative, developmental act rather than a purely retributive one.
points: Punishment should be reserved for one-off, unusual infractions where no pre-established penalty already exists.
The best punishments are designed to make the person more skillful, not merely to inflict discomfort — the piece contrasts an essay assignment with running laps as an example.
A punishment that doesn't match the severity of the infraction is perceived as unjust and breeds resistance rather than learning.
Workplace equivalents of skill-building punishments include coaching or tutoring others, or attending training tied to the infraction, rather than generic busywork.
quotes: Good leaders rely on punishments only when the infraction is a one-off, unusual, or totally unexpected.
As any good parent can tell you, designing punishments is a creative act that requires a lot of thought and consideration.
They insist that the punishment must make the person more skillful or add value to their pre-existing talents.
By asking the transgressor to compose an essay, the student improves their writing and thinking skills, while also learning that actions have consequences.
Punishments that make people more skillful are superior to those that don’t.
